references.text: The Sabbath commandment in the Ten Commandments, which the Pharisees cite when they accuse the disciples of doing something not allowed on the Sabbath.
The Sabbath commandment repeated in Deuteronomy, forbidding work on the Sabbath day – the basis for the Pharisees' objection.
The law permitted picking grain from another's field by hand, but the Pharisees believed this was forbidden on the Sabbath.
The Sabbath commandment that includes a prohibition against working even during plowing and harvest times, which the Pharisees extended to include picking grain.
The parallel passage in Matthew where the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath and the Pharisees react with the same accusation that they are doing something not allowed.
The parallel passage in Mark where the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath and the Pharisees ask Jesus why they are doing what is not allowed on the Sabbath.
The Pharisees again ask whether it is permitted to heal on the Sabbath – the same kind of question about what is lawful on the Sabbath.
Later in the same chapter, the Pharisees keep watch on Jesus to see if he heals on the Sabbath, showing their focus on Sabbath rules.
The synagogue leader reacts with anger when Jesus heals on the Sabbath and says there are six days for work – the same kind of objection about what is allowed.
The Jews tell the healed man that it is not permitted to carry his bed on the Sabbath – the same expression that something 'is not allowed' on the Sabbath.
Some Pharisees say that Jesus cannot be from God because he does not keep the Sabbath – the same kind of accusation from the Pharisees.
